exhibit.title: The School of Athens

exhibitReview.method: Gallery 01 supplemental review: object identity, claims, sources, rights, accessibility, provenance, subject-specific structured interpretation, and aspect-safe object-led presentation.
exhibitReview.resolution: Resolved: replaced the mismatched 2026 AI illustration with Wilfredor’s CC0 photograph of Raphael’s actual fresco; reconciled its records; restored a claim-mapped canon-and-composition sidebar; and matched the 3D frame to the complete photograph.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: Raphael gathers thinkers from many periods into an imagined Renaissance assembly. The central pairing of Plato and Aristotle gives visual order to a much more varied ancient inheritance.

items.label: Central pair
items.description: Plato and Aristotle give the composition a legible center through their books, gestures, and movement.

items.label: Invented assembly
items.description: Raphael joins thinkers from different centuries and traditions inside one Renaissance architectural vision.

items.label: Compressed time
items.description: The harmonious gathering makes historical separation and disagreement less visible.

items.label: Selective inheritance
items.description: The fresco celebrates ancient learning while showing how later cultures decide who occupies its center.

exhibitReview.method: Gallery 01 supplemental review: object identity, claims, sources, rights, accessibility, provenance, subject-specific structured interpretation, and aspect-safe object-led presentation.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: The Ionic Stoa belongs to later phases of Miletus and has been partly restored. The photograph nevertheless places Milesian philosophy in the coastal Anatolian city with which its earliest figures are associated.

items.label: Later fabric
items.description: The restored stoa belongs to later phases of Miletus, not the sixth-century city known to the Milesians.

items.label: Coastal setting
items.description: The remains locate inquiry within an Ionian port shaped by maritime travel, craft, and exchange.

items.label: Shared setting
items.description: Thales, Anaximander, and Anaximenes are associated with Miletus, though their writings survive chiefly through later testimony.

items.label: Different accounts
items.description: Their proposals revise one another rather than forming a single fixed Milesian doctrine.

exhibit.title: The Trial and Death of Socrates

exhibitReview.method: Gallery 01 supplemental review: object identity, claims, sources, rights, accessibility, provenance, subject-specific structured interpretation, and aspect-safe object-led presentation.
exhibitReview.resolution: Resolved: replaced the unverified generated trial scene with Fabre’s authenticated 1802 reception painting; separated event from reception; restored a claim-mapped event-and-reception sidebar; and matched the 3D frame to the complete photograph.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: Fabre’s 1802 painting draws on the literary tradition of Socrates’ final hours. Its calm central figure helped make the philosopher’s death an enduring image of conviction under pressure.

items.label: Ancient event
items.description: Socrates was tried and executed at Athens in 399 BCE; surviving accounts are literary works by followers.

items.label: Modern reception
items.description: Fabre’s 1802 painting turns those accounts into a later moral drama rather than an eyewitness scene.

items.label: Philosophical duty
items.description: Plato’s Apology presents Socrates as refusing to abandon examination in exchange for safety.

items.label: Contested record
items.description: The sources differ in purpose, and the prosecution’s political background remains debated.

exhibit.title: The Allegory of the Cave

exhibitReview.method: Gallery 01 supplemental review: object identity, claims, sources, rights, accessibility, provenance, subject-specific structured interpretation, and aspect-safe object-led presentation.
exhibitReview.resolution: Resolved: restored the approved portrait-format Museum interpretive illustration; identified it honestly as contemporary interpretation; corrected its presentation metadata; and restored a claim-mapped ascent, education, and return sidebar while retaining its natural 4:5 wall format.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: This contemporary Museum illustration places the prisoners, shadow-making objects, cave, and sunlit world in one vertical composition. It interprets Plato’s argument rather than documenting an ancient place or object.

items.label: Below ground
items.description: Prisoners encounter shadows and echoes within a field they have never been able to test.

items.label: Toward the light
items.description: The ascent proceeds by painful adjustment rather than one effortless leap into knowledge.

items.label: Turning the soul
items.description: Education redirects attention and desire toward better objects of understanding.

items.label: Civic obligation
items.description: The person who ascends is required to return, linking knowledge to Plato’s contested case for philosopher-rule.

exhibit.title: Plato’s Republic

exhibitReview.method: Gallery 01 supplemental review: object identity, claims, sources, rights, accessibility, provenance, subject-specific structured interpretation, and aspect-safe object-led presentation.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: Copied around 900 CE, this Greek manuscript preserves the opening of the Republic and gives material form to the long history through which Plato’s dialogue reached later readers.

items.label: Byzantine copy
items.description: Codex Parisinus graecus 1807 was copied around 900 CE, long after Plato composed the dialogue.

items.label: Textual survival
items.description: The page is evidence for the Republic’s transmission, not Plato’s handwriting or an ancient original.

items.label: City and soul
items.description: The city in speech enlarges the question of justice before the dialogue returns to reason, spirit, and appetite in a person.

items.label: Political risk
items.description: Guardian education and philosopher-rule join ethical order to hierarchy, concentrated authority, and coercive institutions.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: The 1643 print imagines the proposal scene through Dutch book illustration. It is evidence for Hipparchia and Crates in later reception, not for their physical appearance or the literal form of their encounter.

items.label: Reported decision
items.description: Later testimony presents Hipparchia as rejecting wealthy suitors and choosing Crates’s way of life.

items.label: Shared practice
items.description: Her remembered public argument and Cynic dress make partnership part of philosophical practice.

items.label: Late testimony
items.description: The main narrative is not eyewitness biography and preserves no secure transcript of the proposal.

items.label: Gendered canon
items.description: Uncertainty should qualify the account without erasing a woman whom the surviving tradition already marginalizes.

exhibit.title: Cynic Cosmopolitanism

exhibitReview.method: Gallery 02 supplemental review: object identity, claims, source mapping, rights, accessibility, provenance, subject-specific structured interpretation, and aspect-safe object-led presentation.
exhibitReview.resolution: Resolved: recast the portrait grid as nineteenth-century reception, separated the Cynic saying from later Stoic theory, restored a claim-mapped phrase-and-lineage sidebar, and matched the wall frame to the complete print.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: Cook’s 1825 grid turns philosophers from different periods into a single printed canon. It contains imagined portraits and a later taxonomy, not evidence for a formal Cynic succession.

items.label: Critical refusal
items.description: Diogenes’s attributed kosmopolitēs reply refuses to let one polis or inherited status define the whole person.

items.label: No world-state
items.description: The fragment does not set out a government, constitution, or complete theory of global citizenship.

items.label: Printed canon
items.description: Cook’s grid makes different periods and disputed affiliations appear settled and simultaneous.

items.label: Later system
items.description: Stoic cosmopolitanism developed claims about nature, law, and obligation that should not be read back into the brief Cynic saying.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: Van Mol’s early-modern painting gives the lamp anecdote a dramatic cast and audience. It documents Diogenes’s later visual reception, not his appearance or a witnessed ancient event.

items.label: Public gesture
items.description: The daylight search stages criticism before an audience rather than offering a literal census of honest people.

items.label: Practiced freedom
items.description: Cynic frank speech gains force from training that reduces dependence on possessions, rank, and approval.

items.label: Late report
items.description: Diogenes Laertius preserves the lamp story centuries after Diogenes lived.

items.label: Reception image
items.description: Van Mol’s painting shows the anecdote’s later visual power, not the appearance of an ancient event.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: The photographed block belongs to Diogenes of Oinoanda’s public Epicurean inscription. It materializes philosophical teaching in civic space but does not contain the fourfold-remedy wording.

items.label: Civic address
items.description: Diogenes of Oinoanda placed Epicurean teaching where citizens, visitors, and later readers could encounter it.

items.label: Connected therapy
items.description: Arguments about nature, mortality, pleasure, and desire support the ethical promise rather than functioning as detached slogans.

items.label: What survives
items.description: The photographed block preserves part of the monumental inscription and its ambition to teach durably in public.

items.label: What remains open
items.description: This block does not contain the fourfold-remedy wording, and scattered fragments cannot recover one complete wall without editorial reconstruction.

exhibitReview.method: Gallery 02 supplemental review: object identity, claims, source mapping, rights, accessibility, provenance, subject-specific structured interpretation, and aspect-safe object-led presentation.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: Castrucci’s diagram explains the mechanism used to open fragile carbonized rolls. It belongs to their eighteenth- and nineteenth-century conservation history, not to the ancient library itself.

items.label: Controlled opening
items.description: Piaggio’s mechanism opened carbonized rolls gradually, but their adhered layers could still split, peel, or crumble.

items.label: Layered evidence
items.description: Ancient ink, early copies, damaged surfaces, modern editions, and editorial inference must remain distinguishable.

items.label: Imaging
items.description: Noninvasive techniques can reveal more data while introducing choices about contrast, alignment, and sequence.

items.label: Attribution
items.description: The Villa holds many Epicurean and Philodemean texts, but not every roll belongs to that school or author.

exhibit.title: Pyrrho in the Storm

exhibitReview.method: Gallery 02 supplemental review: object identity, claims, source mapping, rights, accessibility, provenance, subject-specific structured interpretation, and aspect-safe object-led presentation.
exhibitReview.resolution: Resolved: identified the Pyrrho storm drawing, corrected the anecdote to Diogenes Laertius 9.68, restored a claim-mapped reception-and-practice sidebar, and replaced the portrait wall aperture with the drawing’s natural landscape format.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: The early-modern drawing turns Pyrrho’s storm anecdote into a moral lesson. It is imagined reception, not an ancient likeness, and it should not be mistaken for a diagram of Sextus’s later Pyrrhonism.

items.label: Exemplary calm
items.description: The late anecdote makes Pyrrho point to the untroubled pig while sailors struggle in the storm.

items.label: Reception evidence
items.description: The early-modern drawing shows how the story was moralized, not whether the voyage occurred.

items.label: Contested predecessor
items.description: Pyrrho wrote nothing, and later testimony does not yield a single secure reconstruction of his views.

items.label: Skeptical practice
items.description: Sextus describes opposing considerations, suspending judgment, and continuing through appearances without asserting that nothing can be known.

exhibit.title: The Commentary Classroom: Reading Aristotle Line by Line

exhibitReview.method: Gallery 03 supplemental review: two independent evidence scopes reconciled by the parent across object identity, claims, source mapping, rights, accessibility, provenance, structured interpretation, linking, and aspect-safe presentation.
exhibitReview.resolution: Resolved: identified the displayed 1493 Politics manuscript and qualified shelfmark, separated it from late-antique classroom evidence, and restored sourced interpretation of commentary authorship, method, and concord.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: The 1493 Greek Politics manuscript is a post-Byzantine material witness to Aristotelian transmission. It is not a surviving late-antique classroom copy or the work of a named commentator.

items.label: Layered authorship
items.description: Some Alexandrian commentaries preserve teaching recorded by pupils rather than a single author’s finished book.

items.label: Lemma and problem
items.description: Selecting a passage for exposition frames vocabulary, contradictions, and the larger curricular question to be solved.

items.label: Plato and Aristotle
items.description: Late commentators often argued for harmony between the two philosophers; the harmony was an interpretive achievement, not a given.

items.label: Later material witness
items.description: The 1493 Politics codex shows continued Greek transmission, not the physical setting of a late-antique class.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: The 1385 Glasgow manuscript imagines Boethius first teaching and then imprisoned. Its miniatures are medieval reception, not a likeness or record of his confinement.

items.label: Prison dialogue
items.description: Personified Philosophy addresses a condemned prisoner through alternating argument and poetry.

items.label: Fortune and freedom
items.description: The dialogue connects unstable goods to providence, divine foreknowledge, human freedom, and the highest good.

items.label: Technical vocabulary
items.description: Translation and commentary established Latin distinctions that structured later logical education.

items.label: Uneven inheritance
items.description: Boethius’s Aristotle and Porphyry circulated widely, while his planned translation program remained incomplete.

exhibit.title: Hypatia: Alexandrian Teaching Between Evidence and Legend

exhibitReview.method: Gallery 03 supplemental review: two independent evidence scopes reconciled by the parent across object identity, claims, source mapping, rights, accessibility, provenance, structured interpretation, linking, and aspect-safe presentation.
exhibitReview.resolution: Resolved: identified the 1908 publication object, removed likeness implications, separated contemporary correspondence from later testimony, and mapped teaching, work attribution, murder, and modern reception claims.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: Gaspard’s 1908 printed profile supplies an imagined modern face for Hypatia. It is evidence for her later reception, not her appearance, clothing, or Alexandrian teaching environment.

items.label: Direct address
items.description: Synesius’s Letter 15 is extant contemporary correspondence addressed to Hypatia and witnesses her continuing authority.

items.label: Work attributions
items.description: The Suda links Hypatia to mathematical and astronomical works, but its testimony is much later and requires qualification.

items.label: Socrates, Book VII
items.description: Socrates Scholasticus reports the 415 murder within Alexandrian civic and ecclesiastical conflict.

items.label: Not a complete account
items.description: One narrative source cannot by itself resolve every political motive, responsibility, or later interpretation.

items.label: 1908 publication
items.description: Gaspard’s profile was printed in Little Journeys; it is not derived from an authenticated ancient likeness.

items.label: Reception evidence
items.description: The portrait shows modern demand for a recognizable Hypatia, not what the Alexandrian philosopher looked like.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: The c. 1225 British Library bestiary imagines Aristotle teaching within a later Arabic compilation. It witnesses reception, not an Abbasid translation workshop or Aristotle’s historical classroom.

items.label: Before Islam
items.description: Syriac Christian traditions translated and taught Aristotelian logic and Porphyry before the major Arabic translation movement.

items.label: Beside Arabic
items.description: Syriac translation and scholarship continued alongside Arabic work rather than disappearing after a single handoff.

items.label: Composite source
items.description: The compiler of Kitāb naʿt al-ḥayawān names Aristotle and Ibn Bakhtīshūʿ among the work’s sources.

items.label: Later teaching image
items.description: The c. 1225 miniature imagines Aristotelian authority; it is not a documentary view of translation practice.

items.label: The 1497 collection
items.description: His later collection brought Iamblichus, Proclus, Porphyry, and other Platonist materials together for Latin readers.

exhibit.title: Porphyry’s Isagoge and the Tree That Came Later

exhibitReview.method: Gallery 03 supplemental review: two independent evidence scopes reconciled by the parent across object identity, claims, source mapping, rights, accessibility, provenance, structured interpretation, linking, and aspect-safe presentation.
exhibitReview.resolution: Resolved: qualified the displayed tree’s source-record attribution and date, separated it from Porphyry’s authorship, expanded the claim-mapped interpretation, and preserved its natural proportions.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: The Latin tree is a later visualization of distinctions associated with Porphyry’s Isagoge. Its attribution and date are cautiously reported from the source record; it is not Porphyry’s drawing or an authorial manuscript.

items.label: Kinds of predication
items.description: Genus, species, difference, property, and accident organize the Isagoge’s introduction to Aristotelian logic.

items.label: Questions postponed
items.description: Porphyry declines to decide whether genera and species exist, are bodies, or are separable from sensible particulars.

items.label: Latin curriculum
items.description: Boethius’s translations and commentaries helped carry the Isagoge into long-lived Latin programs of logical study.

items.label: Diagram, not autograph
items.description: The displayed tree is a later classification image; its source record does not make it a drawing by Porphyry.

items.label: Competing willing
items.description: Book VIII presents judgment, habit, and desire pulling the agent in opposing directions immediately before conversion.

items.label: Threefold present

items.label: Recitation test

interpretation.objectInterpretation: Van Delft’s 1400–1404 illumination visualizes the nine angelic choirs in medieval reception. It is not a manuscript of Pseudo-Dionysius or evidence for the corpus’s original setting.

items.label: Scriptural orders

items.label: Pseudonymous authority
items.description: The apostolic persona shaped reception even though scholarship dates the corpus to late antiquity.

interpretation.objectInterpretation: Mir Kalan Khan’s c. 1770–75 Lucknow painting is evidence for a later representation of named holy men. It is not the previously described compendium, an ancient debate, or a comprehensive map of Indian philosophy.

items.label: Named holy men
items.description: The Met identifies a later Lucknow composition of devotional and ascetic figures, not representatives of the six classical schools.

items.label: Constructed encounter
items.description: The arrangement records Mir Kalan Khan’s early-modern act of representation, not a witnessed meeting of every person shown.

items.label: Real disagreement
items.description: Indian traditions offered incompatible accounts of knowledge, self, reality, language, action, and liberation.

items.label: Visible omissions
items.description: One gathering cannot contain the field’s Buddhist, materialist, regional, vernacular, devotional, and scholastic histories.
